title: The Scarlet Letter
author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
description: Puritan Boston in the 1640s, most of it long gone: the scaffold in the market-place, the jail on Prison Lane, Governor Bellingham's glittering hall, and the forest at the edge of the peninsula. Almost every pin here is inferred to its documented site, which is exactly what the certainty labels are for. The frame, The Custom-House, is a real excursion north to Salem, where Hawthorne worked and where the building still stands.

route.summary: Hawthorne frames the novel as a manuscript he claims to have found in the disused upper storey of the Salem Custom-House, wrapped around a faded scrap of gold-embroidered scarlet cloth. The wharf-side building is real and still stands; the found manuscript is the fiction that lets the tale begin.
route.note: The Salem Custom-House where Hawthorne worked as Surveyor is a real building, still standing at Derby Street on Salem's waterfront, some 25 km north of Boston, so it is flagged as an excursion beyond the book's setting.

route.summary: The story issues from the weather-stained oaken door of the town jail, where Hester has been held with her infant. Beside the threshold grows the wild rose-bush Hawthorne plucks a flower from for the reader. The real jail stood on Prison Lane, today's Court Street.
route.note: Hawthorne places the town jail near Cornhill; Boston's first prison stood on Prison Lane, the street now called Court Street, by present-day Court Square. The pin marks that block.

route.summary: Hester is led from the jail to the pillory in the market-place and made to stand three hours before the town, the scarlet letter on her breast and Pearl in her arms. The same scaffold bookends the novel, and it stood on the old town square by the first meeting-house.
route.note: The scaffold of the pillory stood at the western end of the market-place, beneath the eaves of Boston's earliest meeting-house, on the old town square at what is now the corner of Washington and State Streets by the Old State House. The pin marks that square.

route.summary: As he introduces the prison, Hawthorne fixes the young colony by its two earliest civic acts, a jail and a grave. The burial-ground he names on Isaac Johnson's lot is the real one that grew into King's Chapel Burying Ground, the oldest cemetery in Boston.
route.note: Hawthorne names the town's first burial-ground, on Isaac Johnson's lot, as the nucleus of the churchyard of King's Chapel. That ground survives as King's Chapel Burying Ground on Tremont Street, where the pin sits.

route.summary: Hester carries her embroidered gloves to the Governor's stucco-and-glass hall to plead for the right to keep Pearl, whom the magistrates mean to take from her. Bellingham was a real ruler of the colony; the diamond-glittering mansion is Hawthorne's, pinned to the old town.
route.note: Governor Bellingham's mansion is described in the town but its exact site is not documented; Richard Bellingham was a real magistrate and deputy governor of the Massachusetts Bay Colony. The pin sits within the colonial town centre where his household would have stood.

route.summary: In the woods beyond the town, on a mossy trunk by the brook, Hester and Dimmesdale meet alone at last. He forgives her, she unpins the scarlet letter, and for one hour they plan to flee together. The forest is Hawthorne's untamed edge of the Puritan world, drawn rather than mapped.
route.note: The primeval forest where Hester and Dimmesdale meet is generic wilderness beyond the settlement, not a named spot. The pin marks the western edge of the old Shawmut peninsula, at what is now Boston Common, where the town gave way to open land and woods.
